name: Smellmaxxing

lead: Smellmaxxing means improving how you smell, through hygiene, deodorant, diet or fragrance, on the idea that scent adds to attractiveness. A forum thread has asked whether good smell can compensate for looks.

Most body odour comes from bacteria acting on secretions of apocrine glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits. Genetics, notably the ABCC11 gene, and diet also affect odour. Studies report that women tend to prefer the scent of men whose immune genes differ from their own, and that fruit and vegetable intake was linked to sweat described as more pleasant.

paras: People shower regularly, use deodorant or antiperspirant, wash clothes and bedding, care for oral hygiene and choose a fragrance. Deodorants reduce odour, while antiperspirants block sweat pores temporarily. Results are immediate on application.

No notable harms are documented for ordinary hygiene or fragrance use in the sources reviewed. Studies on scent and attraction are small and do not establish how much scent affects perceived attractiveness.

angle.text: Smellmaxxing manages body scent with hygiene, deodorant and fragrance so you smell fresher and come across as more attractive up close. The effect is immediate; body-odour science describes bacteria, genes and diet as the main contributors.

lead: Smellmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for optimising body scent as part of overall attractiveness. It is a minor topic in appearance communities and the available published source material on the term itself is thin.

Reference material on body odour states that the main contribution comes from bacterial activity on skin gland secretions, with diet, sex, health and medication also playing roles.[1] Studies discussed in the same reference report that women tend to prefer the scent of men whose immune genes differ from their own, and that fruit and vegetable intake was linked to sweat described as more pleasant.[1]
infobox: Skin bacteria acting on apocrine secretions

paras: Apocrine glands become active at puberty and produce most compounds that skin flora break down into odour molecules, with Corynebacterium species producing lipases that create smelly acids; different bacteria dominate in men and women.[1]

The ABCC11 gene largely determines underarm odour and earwax type. A non-functional variant reduces body odour in people who carry two copies; it is common in East Asian populations (about 80 to 95 percent) and rare in European and African populations (0 to 3 percent).[1] A 2017 study found that men who ate more fruits and vegetables had sweat rated as more pleasant.[1]

Deodorants reduce odour without reducing sweating, usually with alcohol, antibacterial agents and perfume; antiperspirants, including prescription aluminium chloride types, temporarily block sweat pores.[1]

A 2005 study reported that women tend to prefer the scent of men with immune genes (MHC/HLA) different from their own, and a 2016 study linked HLA to partnership and sexual satisfaction.[1] A 2006 Swedish brain-imaging study found differing responses to putative pheromones in heterosexual and homosexual men and in lesbian women, without establishing cause or effect.[1] A 2012 study showed people can distinguish body odours of different age groups.[1]

No studies found testing smellmaxxing as a looksmaxxing practice or its effect on perceived attractiveness. Related research on body odour and partner preference is described above and is not specific to the term.

The term appears in forum discussions, including a looksmax.org thread asking whether good smells can make up for looks.[2] The discussion in the available source is brief and largely joking, so little can be reliably said about common practices.
